lessons.title: Building a Simple 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast

children.text: This is the single most useful document a cash manager builds, and it fits on one spreadsheet tab. Thirteen weeks is one quarter: long enough to see a problem coming while you can still fix it, short enough that you can name the actual invoices and payments involved. Turnaround professionals reach for it first, and well-run companies keep one running permanently, updated every Monday morning.

body.text: A 13-week forecast is not an accounting exercise. It is a list of the money you expect to receive and pay, by week, so that you find out about the shortfall in week 2 instead of week 6.

children.text: The Shape of It
Every 13-week forecast has the same four blocks, and the arithmetic never changes.

body.caption: Each week's closing balance becomes the next week's opening balance. That chain is the whole model

children.text: Opening balance.
The actual bank balance today, including any overdraft drawn. Start from the bank statement, never from the ledger.
Receipts.
Money expected in, listed by source: named customers first, then other inflows such as a loan drawdown, a GST refund or a deposit returned.
Payments.
Money expected out, grouped so that fixed and statutory items stand out from discretionary ones.
Closing balance.
The result, compared every week against your sanctioned limit.

body.text: Weeks, not months, are the point. A month that nets to positive can still contain a week where payroll on the 1st and GST on the 20th land before the big collection on the 25th. Monthly forecasting hides exactly the failure you are trying to prevent.

children.text: Six Weeks of a Real Forecast
Here are the first six weeks of Konkan Ceramics' forecast, in ₹ lakh, starting from an actual bank balance of ₹12 lakh. The remaining seven weeks work identically.

children.text: Read what the forecast has just done. In week 1, it told the management team that week 6 ends ₹20 lakh overdrawn against a ₹25 lakh limit. There are five weeks to do something about it, and the options are all cheap at this stage: move the capex, chase a specific customer, ask the glaze supplier for 15 days. By week 6 itself, the only options left are expensive ones.

body.title: Forecast closing balance across all 13 weeks (₹ lakh)

series.label: Downside: largest customer pays two weeks late

body.text: The downside line is the one that matters. Slip a single ₹12 lakh collection from week 4 to week 6, which happens constantly, and the trough moves from minus ₹20 lakh to minus ₹32 lakh, which is ₹7 lakh beyond the sanctioned limit. Cheques start bouncing. One late payment by one customer is the difference between a tight quarter and a banking incident.

body.title: Roll the balance forward
body.prompt: Week 5 opens with ₹19 lakh in the bank. Collections of ₹16 lakh are expected and payments of ₹30 lakh are scheduled, including payroll. What is the closing balance for week 5, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: 19 plus 16 minus 30 is ₹5 lakh, which becomes week 6's opening balance. That chaining is the entire mechanic of the model, and it is why an error in one week quietly moves every week after it.

children.text: Filling In the Numbers Honestly
The structure takes an hour. The forecast quality lives entirely in how you estimate the receipts, and that is where most attempts fail.

body.title: How to estimate collections without fooling yourself

children.text: Do not take the invoice due date and assume payment arrives on it. Almost no Indian buyer pays on the due date, and the ones who do are already known to you.
Start with the ageing report, customer by customer.
For the top 20 customers, who together are usually 80% of the book, forecast individually.
Use each customer's own payment history.
If a dealer has paid on day 75 for the last six invoices, forecast day 75, not day 60, however clearly the terms say 60.
Ask sales to confirm the big ones weekly.
Has the invoice been approved, is it in their payment run, is anything disputed?
Forecast the remaining small customers as a single pooled number,
based on the historical percentage collected each week. Individual accuracy there is not worth the effort.
Never include a collection you are hoping for.
A forecast is not a target, and mixing the two destroys its usefulness within a month.

The same discipline applies to payments, in reverse. Include every statutory due date whether or not anyone has reminded you, include the EMI from the sanction letter, and include capex on the payment milestone rather than the approval date.

body.title: What makes a forecast useful, and what kills it

columns.label: Useful
points: Built on weeks, with actual bank balance as the starting point
Collections forecast by named customer using payment history
Every statutory date included by default
One owner, updated the same day each week
Last week's forecast compared against what actually happened
A downside case sitting next to the base case

columns.label: Fatal
points: Monthly totals that hide the mid-month trough
Optimistic sales targets used as receipts
Rebuilt from scratch occasionally, by whoever is free
No comparison of forecast against actual, ever
A single case presented as certainty

body.text: Compare forecast against actual every week, line by line, for the week just gone. It feels tedious for about a month, and then it becomes the most valuable habit in the finance function, because you learn precisely which customers and which departments are systematically optimistic, and you can correct for them.

body.title: Where the forecast starts
body.textWithBlank: The opening balance in week 1 of a cash forecast should come from the actual ___ statement, not from the accounting ledger.
body.explanation: The ledger contains cheques issued but not presented, and receipts recorded but not cleared. The bank statement is the only number that tells you what can actually be spent, and reconciling the two differences is often the first thing a new forecast uncovers.

body.title: Week 6 is coming
body.question: Your forecast shows week 6 closing at minus ₹20 lakh against a ₹25 lakh limit, driven mainly by a ₹15 lakh capex payment. It is currently week 1. Which action deals with the problem most cheaply?
options: Delay the PF and ESI payment due in week 6 by two weeks
Ask the equipment vendor to shift delivery and payment to week 9, and confirm it in writing this week
Wait until week 5 and then request a temporary overdraft enhancement
Stop paying suppliers from week 4 onwards until the balance recovers
body.explanation: Capex is the most movable large item in the list, and five weeks of notice is enough for a vendor to reschedule without penalty. Statutory dues carry interest and penalties, a temporary limit requested at the last minute is expensive and may be refused, and blanket supplier delays hit micro and small suppliers with the consequences from Lesson 3.2.

body.title: Your first Monday running the forecast
body.scenario: You have just been asked to own the weekly cash forecast at a ₹40 crore turnover manufacturer. There is no existing forecast. The finance head wants something on his desk in two weeks. Sales has a receivables ageing report, procurement has purchase orders in a different system, HR runs payroll on the 1st, and nobody has ever been asked for payment dates before.
body.prompt: What do you build in week one, what do you ask for, and what do you deliberately leave out?
body.modelAnswer:
Week one, build the skeleton and populate it roughly.
1. Open a spreadsheet with 13 week-columns and the four blocks: opening balance, receipts, payments, closing balance. Do not buy software yet.
2. Take the opening balance from the bank statement, including the drawn overdraft, and reconcile it once against the ledger so you know the difference.
3. Load every payment you already know with certainty: payroll on the 1st, TDS on the 7th, PF and ESI on the 15th, GST on the 20th, EMIs from the sanction letter, rent on its due date. This alone usually covers 40% to 50% of outflows and needs nobody else's cooperation.
4. Load the top 20 customers from the ageing report and forecast each one on its own payment history, not its terms. Pool the rest as one line.
What to ask for, and from whom.
5. Sales: a weekly call-over of the top 20 collections, with approval status and disputes. Ask for it as a five-minute standing item, not a report.
6. Procurement: open purchase orders with expected delivery and agreed terms, plus anything above a threshold coming in the next quarter.
7. HR: payroll by month including joiners, increments and any bonus or full and final settlements.
8. Projects: capex milestones with expected payment dates.
What to leave out on purpose.
9. Precision beyond one decimal place, or amounts below a materiality threshold such as ₹50,000. They add work and change nothing.
10. Weeks 14 to 52. That is the indirect annual forecast from Lesson 4.1, a different document.
11. Anything you are hoping for: an unsigned order, a pending refund, a possible loan that has not been sanctioned. Put those in a downside or upside case, not the base case.
Then set the rhythm.
12. Update every Monday with the actual bank balance, compare last week's forecast against actual line by line, and circulate one page: the trough, the week it falls in, and the headroom against the limit.
13. Expect the first four weeks to be wrong. Accuracy comes from the variance review, not from the initial build.

body.title: Build yours this week
steps: Create 13 week-columns, starting from the actual bank balance including any overdraft drawn.
Enter fixed statutory payments on their due dates for all 13 weeks: payroll, TDS, PF and ESI, GST and advance tax.
Enter EMIs and lease payments from the sanction letters and agreements.
Forecast the top 20 customers individually using their own payment history, and pool the rest.
Enter supplier payments from the payables ageing and open purchase orders, respecting MSME timelines.
Add capex on its payment milestones, not its approval date.
Chain the closing balances, then mark the lowest point and the week it occurs.
Compare that trough against your sanctioned limits and note the headroom.
Build one downside case: the largest customer pays two weeks late, and see whether the trough breaches the limit.
Fix a weekly update slot, and each week compare the previous week's forecast against actual before touching the new numbers.

cards.definition: A weekly, direct-method projection of receipts and payments over one quarter.
The actual bank balance including drawn overdraft. Always taken from the bank statement.
The lowest forecast closing balance across the period. The number that must fit inside your limits.
The gap between the trough and the sanctioned limit. Your margin for things going wrong.
The same forecast with one realistic thing going wrong, usually a large customer paying late.
The weekly comparison of predicted against actual, line by line. The habit that makes forecasts accurate.

points: Thirteen weeks is long enough to act and short enough to name real invoices and payments. Build it weekly, never monthly.
Closing balance equals opening plus receipts minus payments, chained week to week from the actual bank statement.
Konkan Ceramics' forecast found a ₹20 lakh trough in week 6 while it was still week 1, when fixing it was cheap.
Forecast collections from each customer's payment history, not from invoice due dates, and never from sales targets.
Always run a downside case. One ₹12 lakh collection slipping two weeks turned a ₹5 lakh cushion into a ₹7 lakh limit breach.
Compare forecast against actual every week. That review, not the model, is what makes the numbers trustworthy.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional and all figures are illustrative. Statutory due dates are simplified and can change. Confirm current requirements with your chartered accountant or finance team.
